intro: Six matriculation-exam-style problems bring together the photons, atoms, nuclei and radiation of the lesson. Solve them as in the exam: name the phenomenon and the model and justify why the model fits the situation, solve for the quantity asked before substituting numbers, and assess whether the result is reasonable. Open the model answer and the marking scheme only when your solution is ready.

tasks.title: Caesium in forest mushrooms
tasks.source_note: The activity concentrations of the mushrooms are an invented example. The half-life of caesium-137, the gamma photon energy $662\,\text{keV}$ and the adult dose coefficient $1.3 \cdot 10^{-8}\,\tfrac{\text{Sv}}{\text{Bq}}$ are real values.
tasks.text:
The fallout of the Chernobyl accident left caesium-137 in Finnish forests, and it accumulates especially in mushrooms. Caesium-137 decays by beta minus decay into barium-137m, which is an excited nucleus of barium. It returns to the ground state by emitting a gamma photon whose energy is $662\,\text{keV}$. In a forest area in the Häme region, the caesium-137 concentration of funnel chanterelles was measured in 1990 as $2400\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{kg}}$ fresh weight.

- atomic number of caesium $55$, of barium $56$
- half-life of caesium-137 $30.1\,\text{a}$, $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$
- dose coefficient: one ingested becquerel of caesium-137 gives an adult an effective dose of $1.3 \cdot 10^{-8}\,\text{Sv}$
- the average effective dose of a person in Finland is about $5.9\,\text{mSv}$ per year
- assume that caesium leaves the mushrooms only by decaying

parts.text: Write the equations of the decay of caesium-137 and the de-excitation of barium-137m. How large is the wavelength of the gamma photon?

criteria.text: Writes ${}^{137}_{55}\text{Cs} \to {}^{137}_{56}\text{Ba}^{\ast} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} + \bar{\nu}$ and ${}^{137}_{56}\text{Ba}^{\ast} \to {}^{137}_{56}\text{Ba} + \gamma$ so that the mass number and the charge number are conserved.

parts.text: How large is the caesium-137 concentration of the same mushrooms in 2026?

criteria.text: Justifies that the activity decreases according to the decay law, because each nucleus decays with the same probability and no new caesium comes in.

parts.text: During 2026 a mushroom picker eats $5.0\,\text{kg}$ of such mushrooms. How large an effective dose does the picker get from the mushrooms? Compare the dose with the average annual dose of a person in Finland.

criteria.detail: ingested activity $A m$ and dose $H_\text{E} = A m \cdot k$, where $k$ is the dose coefficient
About $1\,\%$ of the average $5.9\,\text{mSv}$, so the share of the mushrooms is small.

parts.text: How many caesium-137 nuclei are there in one kilogram of mushrooms in 2026, and how large is their mass? The mass of a caesium-137 atom is $137\,\text{u}$, $1\,\text{u} = 1.66 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$.

criteria.detail: $A = \lambda N$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$, so $N = \dfrac{A T_{1/2}}{\ln 2}$; mass $m = N \cdot 137\,\text{u}$

tasks.title: Hydrogen lines in a distant galaxy
tasks.source_note: The galaxy and the wavelength of its spectrum are an invented example. The laboratory values $656.3\,\text{nm}$ and $486.1\,\text{nm}$ of the hydrogen lines are real.
tasks.text:
On an upper secondary astronomy course, students study the spectrum of a distant galaxy measured with the spectrograph of a telescope. The spectrum has dark lines, and the strongest of them is identified as the red line of hydrogen.

- energy levels of the hydrogen atom $E_n = -\tfrac{13.6\,\text{eV}}{n^2}$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
- wavelength of the red line of hydrogen in the laboratory $656.3\,\text{nm}$ and of the cyan line $486.1\,\text{nm}$
- in the spectrum of the galaxy the red line is at the wavelength $671.8\,\text{nm}$
- Hubble constant $H_0 = 70\,\tfrac{\text{km/s}}{\text{Mpc}}$, speed of light $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{5}\,\text{km/s}$

parts.text: The red line of hydrogen arises in the transition from level $3$ to level $2$. Calculate the wavelength of the line from the levels.

criteria.text: Justifies that the photon energy is the difference of the levels $E_3 - E_2$, because energy is conserved in the transition.

parts.text: At what speed is the galaxy receding from us, and how far away is it?

criteria.text: Justifies that the line has shifted to longer wavelengths because the galaxy recedes as space expands, and that the redshift is small, so $v = cz$ holds.

criteria.detail: $v \approx 7.1 \cdot 10^{3}\,\text{km/s}$ and $d \approx 100\,\text{Mpc}$, two significant figures like the Hubble constant

parts.text: At what wavelength does the cyan line of hydrogen appear in the spectrum of the galaxy?

criteria.text: Justifies that the redshift $z$ is the same for every line of the spectrum.

parts.text: Explain why the hydrogen lines in the spectrum of the galaxy are dark and not bright.

criteria.text: Explains that the hot surface of the stars emits a continuous spectrum, and the outermost gas layers of the stars lie between it and the observer.
Explains that hydrogen atoms absorb only photons whose energy is exactly the difference of levels, and re-emit the energy in all directions.

criteria.detail: The light coming towards the observer lacks exactly the wavelengths of hydrogen, so the lines are darker than their surroundings.

tasks.title: The photoelectric effect and the Planck constant
tasks.source_note: The voltages have been calculated from the photoelectric equation, and variation like that of measurements has been added to them.
tasks.text:
In a physics lab a photocell whose cathode is potassium is studied. When the cathode is lit, electrons leave it and travel through a vacuum to the anode, and a photocurrent flows in the circuit. A voltage that slows the electrons down is connected between the anode and the cathode: the anode is more negative than the cathode. The voltage is increased until the photocurrent just stops. This voltage is called the stopping voltage $U$. The cathode was lit in turn with different wavelengths using an LED light source and filters.

| $\lambda\ (\text{nm})$ | $U\ (\text{V})$ |
|---|---|
| $365$ | $1.15$ |
| $405$ | $0.80$ |
| $436$ | $0.61$ |
| $470$ | $0.38$ |
| $505$ | $0.21$ |
| $590$ | no current |

- $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$

parts.text: Present the stopping voltage as a function of the frequency of the light as a graph.

criteria.detail: $f\ (10^{14}\,\text{Hz})$ on the horizontal axis, $U\ (\text{V})$ on the vertical axis; axes named and units marked.

criteria.text: Does not plot a point for the wavelength $590\,\text{nm}$, because no photocurrent arises there, and does not join the points into a broken line.

parts.text: Justify why a straight line fits the points, and fit a straight line to the points. Extend the line so that it crosses both axes.

criteria.text: Justifies with conservation of energy: the kinetic energy $E_\text{k,max}$ of the fastest electron is used up entirely in the braking work done by the electric field, so $eU = E_\text{k,max}$.
Combines this with the photoelectric equation: $eU = hf - W$, so $U = \dfrac{h}{e}\,f - \dfrac{W}{e}$ is the equation of a straight line.

criteria.detail: One straight line between the points, extended as a dashed line to the vertical axis and to the horizontal axis.

parts.text: Determine the Planck constant from the graph. Compare the result with the value $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(0;\ -2.24\,\text{V})$ and $(8.0 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz};\ 1.06\,\text{V})$: $k \approx 4.13 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$

criteria.text: Interprets the slope: $k = \dfrac{h}{e}$.

criteria.detail: Compares the difference with the table value $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$ and assesses whether it is within the reading accuracy of the graph.

parts.text: Determine from the graph the work function of potassium in electronvolts and the threshold frequency. Explain why no photocurrent arises at the wavelength $590\,\text{nm}$, and whether the situation would change if there were ten times more $590\,\text{nm}$ light.

criteria.detail: The line crosses the vertical axis at $-\tfrac{W}{e} \approx -2.24\,\text{V}$ and the horizontal axis at $f_0 \approx 5.43 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$.

criteria.text: Calculates that the frequency $5.08 \cdot 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}$ of $590\,\text{nm}$ is smaller than the threshold frequency, that is, the photon energy $2.10\,\text{eV}$ is smaller than the work function.

criteria.detail: Brighter light brings more photons but not more energetic ones, so still no electrons leave.

tasks.title: Radon at the housing company meeting
tasks.source_note: The meeting and the measurement result are an invented example. The reference level $300\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$ for the radon concentration of dwellings follows the Finnish Radiation Act.
tasks.text:
In the flats of a terraced-house company in Hyvinkää, the radon concentration was measured in winter for two months. The result of one flat was $450\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$. At the residents' meeting three claims were made.

1. “The alpha radiation of radon is stopped by paper and by the surface of the skin, so it cannot be dangerous.”
2. “The half-life of radon is only $3.8$ days. If we keep the windows tightly shut for a month, the radon will disappear by itself.”
3. “The neighbour had a dental X-ray. Now she is radioactive too, so the children should not be near her.”

The reference level for the radon concentration of dwellings is $300\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$. Radon-222 forms from radium in the decay series of uranium in the soil and bedrock.

parts.text: Assess claim 1. Explain how radon causes a radiation dose.

criteria.text: States that alpha radiation does not penetrate the skin, so external alpha radiation is not dangerous; that part of the claim's justification is true.
Explains that radon and its decay products are breathed into the lungs, where the alpha radiation hits the cells of the lungs directly.
Justifies the danger: an alpha particle ionises densely and gives up its energy over a distance of a few cells, and its weighting factor is $20$.

criteria.detail: The claim is false: radon is the largest source of radiation dose for people in Finland, and $450\,\tfrac{\text{Bq}}{\text{m}^3}$ is $1.5$ times the reference level, so the concentration should be reduced.

parts.text: Assess claim 2. According to the model, what fraction of the radon nuclei in the room is still undecayed after a month, and does the radon still disappear from the flat?

criteria.detail: $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{30 : 3.8} \approx 0.004$, that is about $0.4\,\%$ of the original radon nuclei

criteria.text: States that the calculation holds only for the nuclei that were in the room at the start.
Explains that the uranium decay series in the soil produces radon all the time, and it flows in through cracks in the foundations when the pressure indoors is lower.

criteria.detail: The claim is false: when the windows and ventilation are closed, as much new radon comes in as before but less of it leaves, so the concentration increases. The concentration is reduced by ventilation and by sealing the structures.

parts.text: Assess claim 3.

criteria.text: Explains that X-rays are photon radiation that either passes through the tissue or is absorbed and ionises atoms during the imaging.
Justifies that radioactivity is a property of unstable nuclei, and the energy of an X-ray photon, about $60\,\text{keV}$, ionises atoms but does not change nuclei.
Distinguishes external exposure from radioactive material entering the body: only the latter makes a person a radiation source, as a tracer of a nuclear medicine examination does for a short time.

criteria.detail: The claim is false: when the X-ray unit switches off, there is no radiation any more, and no radiation comes from the neighbour to the children.

tasks.title: The half-life of barium-137m
tasks.source_note: The report and the measurements are an invented example. The readings have been calculated with a half-life of $153\,\text{s}$ and a background of $5$ counts in $10\,\text{s}$, and variation like the randomness of decay has been added to them.
tasks.text:
A group of students measured the half-life of barium-137m. The barium solution was eluted from an isotope generator into a sample dish, and the dish was placed under a GM tube. The counts were recorded in $10\,\text{s}$ periods every $30\,\text{s}$. Before the measurement the background radiation was measured once for $10\,\text{s}$, giving $5$ counts.

| $t\ (\text{s})$ | counts $/\ 10\,\text{s}$ |
|---|---|
| $0$ | $398$ |
| $30$ | $361$ |
| $60$ | $304$ |
| $90$ | $276$ |
| $120$ | $231$ |
| $150$ | $212$ |
| $180$ | $188$ |
| $210$ | $163$ |
| $240$ | $136$ |
| $270$ | $127$ |
| $300$ | $104$ |

The group's conclusion: “At the start there were $398$ counts, and half of that, $199$, was reached at about $166\,\text{s}$. So the half-life is $166\,\text{s}$, which is $8\,\%$ more than the book value $153\,\text{s}$. The difference is because the solution stood in the dish for about a minute before the measurement, so the remaining nuclei were older and decayed more slowly. The background did not need to be subtracted, because it was only $5$ counts.”

parts.text: Determine the half-life from the data, taking the background radiation into account.

criteria.text: Subtracts the background from each of the $11$ readings before calculating: $393$ at the start and $99$ at the end, counts in $10\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: $\ln N = \ln N_0 - \lambda t$, so the slope of the line $(t,\ \ln N)$ is $k = -\lambda$ and $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{-k}$; a fit to all the points. The two-point calculation $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{t \ln 2}{\ln (N_0 : N)}$ is also accepted
$k \approx -4.53 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{s}}$ and $T_{1/2} \approx 153\,\text{s}$; about $151\,\text{s}$ with the two-point calculation
The result is within a few per cent of the book value $153\,\text{s}$.

parts.text: Assess the group's conclusion.

criteria.text: States that the explanation is wrong: a nucleus has no age, but every barium-137m nucleus has the same decay probability per second, so standing does not change the half-life.

criteria.detail: The half-life was read from a single reading and by interpolating between two points, so the random variation of decay in one reading affects it directly.
States that the background should have been subtracted: a background measured once is uncertain, and its share grows at the end: $5$ counts is about $5\,\%$ of the reading $104$.
The difference $166\,\text{s}$ versus $153\,\text{s}$ comes from the way of measuring and reading, not from the sample; the whole data set gives about $151$–$153\,\text{s}$.

parts.text: Plan how the measurement and the processing of the results can be improved.

criteria.text: Measures the background for a long time, for example $10\,\text{min}$, before or after the measurement and subtracts it from each reading in the same unit.
Uses all the measurement points: fits the model $y = A\,e^{-Ct} + B$ to the points, or draws a graph and determines the half-life from the fitted curve.
Lengthens the counting time or repeats the whole measurement with a new sample and compares the results, so that the random variation decreases and the spread can be seen.

criteria.detail: Estimates the uncertainty of the result from the spread of the repeats or with the fit before comparing it with the book value.

tasks.title: Electricity from a nuclear power plant
tasks.source_note: The powers of the plant are an invented example in the size class of a large pressurised water plant. The heat of combustion of hard coal $24\,\tfrac{\text{MJ}}{\text{kg}}$ is a typical value.
tasks.text:
A Finnish nuclear power plant with a pressurised water reactor has an electric power of $1600\,\text{MW}$ when the thermal power of the reactor is $4300\,\text{MW}$. In the condenser the steam from the turbine condenses, and seawater is pumped in for cooling and warms up by $11\,\text{K}$. Assume that the plant runs at full power for the whole year.

- one fission of uranium-235 releases on average $200\,\text{MeV}$
- mass of a uranium-235 atom $235\,\text{u}$, $1\,\text{u} = 1.661 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$
- specific heat capacity of seawater $4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$
- $1\,\text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{s}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$
- heat of combustion of hard coal $24\,\tfrac{\text{MJ}}{\text{kg}}$, efficiency of a coal power plant $40\,\%$
- assume that all the heat that does not become electricity goes to the seawater in the condenser

parts.text: How large is the efficiency of the plant, and how many fissions happen in the reactor per second?
How many kilograms of uranium-235 undergo fission in a year? How much mass is converted into energy in the same time?

criteria.text: Interprets that only about $0.09\,\%$ of the mass of the fissioned uranium is converted into energy; the rest remains as fission products and neutrons, because the mass number is conserved.

parts.text: How many kilograms of seawater must be pumped through the condenser per second?

criteria.text: Justifies that by conservation of energy the thermal power that does not become electricity, $P_\text{th} - P_\text{e} = 2700\,\text{MW}$, goes to the seawater in the condenser.

parts.text: How many tonnes of hard coal would a coal power plant burn in a year if it produced the same electrical energy?

criteria.detail: $E_\text{e} = P_\text{e} t$ and $E_\text{e} = \eta H m$, so $m = \dfrac{P_\text{e} t}{\eta H}$
About $5$ million tonnes, over three million times the mass of the fissioned uranium, because fission releases about $200\,\text{MeV}$ and burning a few electronvolts per reaction.
